entry: Waterfall system on the Iguazu River, on the border of Argentina and Brazil. The falls divide the river into upper and lower Iguazu, and together they form the largest waterfall system in the world, most of it on the Argentine side. The river rises near [[Curitiba]]. The falls form a two-step staircase over three layers of [[Basalt|basalt]], with steps 35 and 40 m high. Their number ranges from 150 to 300 depending on the water level. About half of the river's flow drops into the Devil's Throat, a canyon 80–90 m wide. The lower river drains into the [[Paraná River]], a short distance downstream from the [[Itaipu Dam]]. The name derives from Guarani or Tupi words meaning *water* and *big*. Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca was the first European to record the falls, in 1541. Iguazú National Park in Argentina and Iguaçu National Park in Brazil protect the site, inscribed as [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]] in 1984 and 1986.

Ancient Greek epic poem attributed to [[Homer]]. It is one of two major surviving Greek epics, along with the [[Odyssey]], and is divided into 24 books written in dactylic hexameter, with 15,693 lines in its standard edition. Set in the final weeks of the [[Trojan War]], a 10-year siege of [[Troy]] by a coalition of Mycenaean Greek states, it focuses on [[Achilles]], whose wrath drives the narrative. The poem does not depict the fall of Troy or mention the [[Trojan Horse]], which later sources describe. Scholars debate its composition, historicity and authorship, and it was likely composed in Homeric Greek between the late 8th and early 7th century. The Greeks esteemed it and taught it as part of their standard education, and professional reciters known as rhapsodes performed it at festivals such as the Panathenaia. It is often regarded as the first substantial piece of European literature and remains central to the study of classical philology.

Anadromous fish related to the [[Herring|herring]], and the national fish of [[Bangladesh]]. It is a very popular, sought-after food in the Bengal region and is also the state fish of [[West Bengal]], India. As of 2023, 97% of the world's total ilish supply originated in Bangladesh, where the fish contributes about 12% of total fish production and about 1.15% of GDP. Around 450,000 people are directly involved in catching it. Ilish feeds on [[Plankton|plankton]] and forages in muddy bottoms. Females grow larger than males, reaching up to 55 cm (22 in). The fish ascends rivers for 50–100 km (31–62 mi) to spawn during the southwest monsoons, and it is found in 11 countries, among them Iran, Iraq and Thailand. Bangladesh is the top hilsa-producing country in the world, followed by Myanmar and then India.

Mongol khanate in western Asia, centered on Iran. It was established after Hülegü, grandson of [[Genghis Khan]], inherited the West and Central Asian parts of the [[Mongol Empire]] in 1259. Its core lay in what are now Iran, Azerbaijan and Turkey. Later rulers, beginning with Ghazan in 1295, converted to [[Islam]]. The Black Death ravaged the state in the 1330s, and after the last ilkhan, Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, died in 1335, the Ilkhanate disintegrated.

Global [[Black market|black market]] for prohibited drugs. It covers the cultivation, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs that prohibition laws forbid, and is also called drug trafficking or narcotrafficking. In 2014 the think tank Global Financial Integrity estimated the illicit drug market at between US$426 and US$652 billion, or nearly 1% of total global trade. [[Tobacco]] and [[Opium]] were the first drugs subjected to prohibitory government legislation. In the 18th century the [[East India Company]] began smuggling Indian opium to Chinese merchants, and the destruction of opium at Humen led to the [[First Opium War]] in 1839. In the early 21st century, syndicates such as the [[Sinaloa Cartel]] increased cooperation to facilitate transatlantic trafficking. Penalties depend on the type and quantity of drug, and where and how it is sold, and can include lengthy incarceration.

[[U.S. state]] in the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]]. Its capital is Springfield, and [[Chicago]] is the largest city. The state borders [[Lake Michigan]] to the northeast and the Mississippi River to the west. Indigenous cultures lived there for thousands of years before French settlers arrived in the 17th century as part of [[New France]]. Illinois achieved statehood in 1818. Its economy is highly diversified, and Chicago is a major transportation hub. Two [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]] lie in the state: the ancient [[Cahokia|Cahokia Mounds]] and part of the Wright architecture site.

Name given to several real and fictitious groups, most often the Bavarian Illuminati, an Enlightenment-era [[Secret society|secret society]]. Founded on 1 May 1776 in the Electorate of [[Bavaria]], it aimed to oppose superstition, religious influence over public life and abuses of state power by monarchs. Charles Theodore, Elector of Bavaria, outlawed it in 1784, 1785, 1787 and 1790, with the encouragement of the [[Catholic Church]]. Conservative critics later claimed that it continued underground and was responsible for the [[French Revolution]], though these links have not been substantiated. Later organizations alleged to continue it have been accused of conspiring to control world affairs.

Decoration, interpretation or visual explanation of a text, concept or process, made for print and digital media. Illustrations appear in posters, magazines, books, teaching materials, animations, video games and films, and are typically made by an illustrator. The art is closely linked to [[Printing|printing]] and publishing. Medieval codices carried hand-painted illuminations, and from the 15th century printed books were often illustrated with woodcuts. [[Ukiyo-e]], an influential style of expressive line and vivid color, originated in 1600s Japan. Specialist areas include botanical, medical, technical and scientific illustration. Once considered less important than graphic design and fine art, illustration is now increasingly valued. *Breaking Home Ties* by [[Norman Rockwell]] sold for US$15.4 million at a 2006 Sotheby's auction.

Ukrainian-born Russian painter. Born in Chuguev, then part of Russia, he became one of the most renowned artists in 19th-century Russia. His major works include *Barge Haulers on the Volga* (1873), *Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan* (1885) and *Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks* (1880–1891). He painted revealing portraits of leading Russian literary and artistic figures, notably [[Leo Tolstoy]], with whom he had a long friendship, and [[Modest Mussorgsky]]. The Ivan painting caused a scandal and was removed from exhibition. In 1898 he built the Penates, a country house in Kuokkala, Finland, now a museum and [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. He quit his teaching post at the Academy of Arts in 1905 after the repression of street demonstrations.

Four-engined turbofan strategic airlifter designed by the [[Soviet Union]]'s Ilyushin design bureau. Conceived in 1967 as a commercial freighter to replace the Antonov An-12, it was built to carry heavy machinery to remote areas. Production was allocated to the Tashkent Aviation Production Association in [[Tashkent]], and some 860 basic transports were built. It can operate from unpaved runways. Military variants serve as an [[Aerial refueling|aerial refueling]] tanker and as the basis of an [[Airborne early warning and control|airborne early warning and control]] aircraft. The Russian Air Force was its primary operator, and in 2005 China ordered 34 new Il-76MD aircraft.

Visual representation, two-dimensional or three-dimensional. Two-dimensional images include drawings, [[Painting|paintings]] and photographs; three-dimensional ones include carvings and sculpture. An image may be displayed by projection, electronic signals or digital displays, and reproduced by printmaking or photocopying. A volatile image exists only briefly, as in a mirror reflection or a [[Camera obscura]] projection, while a fixed image, or hard copy, is recorded on paper or textile. [[Holography]] can create reproducible three-dimensional images that cannot be touched. Mental images exist in the mind and must be conveyed through words or visual productions to be understood by others. The standard for motion pictures has been 24 frames per second since at least the late 1920s.

Device that optically converts images, printed text or objects into a digital image. The most common type for home and office use is the flatbed scanner, on which the document rests on a glass bed. A sheetfed scanner moves paper past the sensor with rollers, and a handheld scanner is a portable version. Scans are usually downloaded to the connected computer, though some store them on standalone [[Memory card|memory cards]] or [[USB]] drives. Modern scanners use a [[Charge-coupled device|charge-coupled device]] (CCD) or contact image sensor (CIS), while drum scanners, developed earlier, use a photomultiplier tube for the highest image quality. Image scanners succeeded early [[Fax|fax]] and wirephoto machines. The earliest fax attempt, patented in 1843 by Scottish clockmaker Alexander Bain, was never put into production.

Product of a real number and the [[Imaginary unit|imaginary unit]] *i*, which is defined by *i*² = −1. For example, 5*i* is imaginary and its square is −25; zero is considered both real and imaginary. [[René Descartes]] coined the term in the 17th century as a derogatory word for what he regarded as fictitious or useless. The concept gained wide acceptance through the work of [[Leonhard Euler]] in the 18th century and of [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] and [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] in the early 19th century. An imaginary number added to a real number forms a [[Complex number|complex number]], *a* + *bi*. Geometrically, imaginary numbers lie on the vertical axis of the complex plane, and multiplying by *i* rotates a point 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin.

Mathematical constant that solves the equation *x*² = −1, usually denoted *i*. Its two square roots, *i* and −*i*, are additive inverses of each other. The powers of *i* cycle through 1, *i*, −1 and −*i*. Historically denoted by the square root of −1, the symbol is now rare. Because *i* denotes electric current, [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineering]] normally writes the unit as *j*. The name imaginary is generally credited to [[René Descartes]], and [[Isaac Newton]] used the term as early as 1670. The *i* notation was introduced by [[Leonhard Euler]]. Combined with real numbers, the unit forms the [[Complex number|complex numbers]] of the form *a* + *bi*.

Last stage of an insect's [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]], the sexually mature adult. The word derives from the [[Latin]] for *image*. It follows the final molt. In species with incomplete metamorphosis it follows the last nymphal stage; in species with a [[Pupa|pupal]] stage it follows emergence from the pupa. The imago is the only stage at which the insect is sexually mature, and in winged species the only stage with functional wings. Mayflies (Ephemeroptera) lack a pupal stage and pass through an intermediate winged stage, the subimago. Entomologists use the Latin plural *imagines*, although *imagoes* is also acceptable.

Leader of congregational prayer in [[Islam]]. In Sunni Islam, an imam is anyone charged with leading formal prayers, including outside mosques whenever two or more people pray; the role is not hereditary or divinely appointed. Women may lead only when no men are present. The title is also an honorary term for scholarly authorities, especially jurists and the founders of the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence. In [[Shia Islam]], imams are infallible leaders after the [[Muhammad|Prophet Muhammad]], and the term applies only to members of the Ahl al-Bayt, his family. Twelver Shia recognize twelve imams among the Fourteen Infallibles and believe that the last, the Mahdi, will emerge on the Day of Resurrection. The title was also used by the Zaidi imams of [[Yemen]].

Somali-born American model and actress. Born in Mogadishu, she was discovered by photographer Peter Beard while studying at the University of Nairobi, and her first assignment for [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] came in 1976. A muse of designers including [[Calvin Klein]], Gianni Versace, Thierry Mugler, Donna Karan and [[Yves Saint Laurent (designer)|Yves Saint Laurent]], she became one of the world's most iconic models and is noted for philanthropic work. She was married to basketball player Spencer Haywood from 1977 to 1987, and to musician David Bowie from 1992 until his death in 2016.

Egyptian chancellor to King Djoser and possible architect of his step pyramid, later deified. Imhotep was also high priest of the sun god [[Ra]] at Heliopolis. Little is known of him as a historical figure, but in the 3,000 years after his death he was glorified as a writer of wisdom texts and especially as a physician. Two contemporary inscriptions confirm that he served as chancellor. Egyptologists credit him with designing the stepped pyramid at Saqqara, built in the 3rd Dynasty, although pharaonic Egyptians never credited him with it. He was among fewer than a dozen non-royal Egyptians deified after death. Equated with [[Thoth]], god of architecture, mathematics and medicine, he was venerated as a god of healing, with his cult centered in Memphis. The location of his tomb remains unknown.

Series of two Japanese invasions of [[Korea]], 1592–1598. The invasions were launched by [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] to conquer Korea, and Japan quickly occupied much of the country. Reinforcements from Ming China and the disruption of Japanese supply fleets by the [[Joseon]] Navy forced the Japanese to withdraw from the northern provinces. Joseon civilian militias then waged guerrilla warfare, and a stalemate followed. After a truce in 1596, Japan invaded again in 1597 in a campaign called the Chŏngyu War, and both sides were locked in a ten-month stalemate. Hideyoshi's death and the Japanese defeat at the naval Battle of Noryang ended the war. Peace negotiations followed for several years, ultimately normalizing relations.

International movement of people to a destination country in which they settle as permanent residents. Commuters, tourists and other short-term visitors are generally excluded from the definition, though a visitor who overstays a visa may become an immigrant. Research suggests that migration can be beneficial to both receiving and sending countries, and the academic literature gives mixed findings on immigration and crime. Immigrants assimilate considerably, although country of origin affects the speed and depth of assimilation. Discrimination based on nationality is legal in most countries, and extensive evidence has found discrimination against foreign-born people in criminal justice, business, housing, health care and politics. As of 2015, international migrants numbered 244 million, a 41% increase since 2000, and the [[United States]] hosted the largest number, 19% of the world's total.

Branch of biology and medicine that studies immune systems in all organisms. It charts the functioning of the immune system in health and disease, including autoimmune diseases, hypersensitivities, immune deficiency and transplant rejection. The term was coined by the Russian biologist Ilya Ilyich Mechnikov, who first observed phagocytosis and shared the 1908 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] with Paul Ehrlich. The earliest written mention of immunity dates to the plague of Athens in 430 BC, recorded by [[Thucydides]]. The immune system is divided into innate immunity and, in vertebrates, adaptive immunity, which has humoral (antibody) and cell-mediated components. [[Antibody|Antibodies]] are proteins released by B lymphocytes that identify targets for destruction rather than killing pathogens directly. The field has applications in organ transplantation, [[Cancer|oncology]], rheumatology, virology and dermatology.

Depression in the surface of a solid astronomical body, formed by the hypervelocity impact of a smaller object. Unlike volcanic craters, impact craters typically have raised rims and floors lower than the surrounding terrain. They range from microscopic pits on lunar rocks to vast, multi-ringed impact basins. Impact craters dominate the surfaces of the [[Moon]], [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] and most small moons and asteroids. On [[Earth]], [[Erosion|erosion]] and other processes destroy most of the record, and about 190 terrestrial impact craters have been identified. Earth experiences, on average, one to three impacts large enough to produce a 20-kilometer-diameter crater every million years. Meteor Crater is a well-known small example. The cratering records of old surfaces show an intense early bombardment about 3.9 billion years ago.

Collision between astronomical objects, causing measurable effects. Most impacts involve [[Asteroid|asteroids]], comets or meteoroids and have minimal effect. Large impacts on [[Terrestrial planet|terrestrial planets]] can have significant consequences; the minimum speed for a body striking [[Earth]] is 11.2 km/s, Earth's escape velocity. The prehistoric Chicxulub impact, 66 million years ago, is believed to have caused the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction]]. The 1908 [[Tunguska event]] occurred in a sparsely populated part of [[Siberia]], Russia. [[Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9]] provided the first direct observation of an extraterrestrial collision when it struck [[Jupiter]] in July 1994. In a 2022 test, the Double Asteroid Redirection Test changed the target's orbital period by 32 minutes, against a success criterion of more than 73 seconds.

Medium-sized [[Antelope|antelope]] of eastern and southern Africa. It is the only living member of the genus *Aepyceros*. It stands 70–92 cm (28–36 in) at the shoulder and weighs 40–65 kg, with a glossy, reddish-brown coat. Only males have slender, lyre-shaped horns, 45–92 cm long. Active mainly by day, impalas form territorial males, bachelor herds and female herds, and are known for two characteristic leaps used as an anti-predator strategy. Their annual rut takes place toward the end of the wet season, typically in May, and gestation lasts six to seven months. The black-faced subspecies is confined to southwestern Angola and Kaokoland in Namibia and is classified as vulnerable, with fewer than 1,000 individuals in the wild as of 2008; the common impala is classified as least concern.

Principle of [[Justice|justice]] holding that decisions should rest on objective criteria, not [[Bias|bias]] or [[Prejudice|prejudice]]. In philosophy, impartiality is a formal property of choices: a choice is impartial when considerations such as who benefits or is harmed have no influence on it. Many moral theories, including [[Utilitarianism]], Kantian ethics and contractualism, treat the impartial point of view as the standpoint from which moral questions are judged. [[David Hume]] held that moral judgments are made from a "common point of view". [[Adam Smith]] described an impartial spectator, and [[John Rawls]] asked which principles rational agents would choose behind a "veil of ignorance". Critics argue that strict impartiality leaves no room for the special concern people show for family and friends, a disagreement known as the partialist–impartialist debate. Impartiality is also a legal standard for courts and public administration.
